title: Soccer Boss in Big Trouble! Two Giant Groups Demand a 'Full Review'
summary: Imagine you're the boss of all soccer in the world. That's Gianni Infantino's job as president of FIFA. But now, two huge soccer groups are saying he's not doing a good job. UEFA (which runs soccer in Europe) and Concacaf (which runs it in North America, Central America, and the Caribbean) both spoke out on Saturday. They're upset about a plan Infantino had to sell shares of FIFA's big tournaments to private investors. That means companies could own a piece of the World Cup! After lots of pushback, Infantino dropped the plan. But the groups say the damage is done. UEFA said Infantino failed to keep his promises to be open and honest. They even quoted a speech he made in 2016, when he said, 'The money of FIFA is your money.' Concacaf was even tougher, calling the plan a 'symptom of leadership that has stopped putting football first' and demanding a 'full review' of his leadership. Only Qatar's soccer group has publicly backed Infantino so far. The UK Prime Minister even said Infantino should quit! With a re-election vote coming in March, Infantino is under huge pressure. Will he keep his job, or will the soccer world force him out? Stay tuned!
why_it_matters: When the boss of a sport you love breaks promises and focuses on money, it can change how the game is run and even affect which countries get to host big tournaments.

background_read: FIFA (the world governing body for soccer) has faced major scandals. In 2015, many of its top officials were arrested for taking bribes, and Gianni Infantino (who became FIFA president in 2016) promised to clean up the organization and be more open.

Selling shares of tournaments like the World Cup to private investors is controversial because some fear the investors would care more about profit than about helping the sport grow in poorer countries. UEFA and Concacaf are two of the six regional confederations that make up FIFA.
Article_Structure: WHO: Gianni Infantino, UEFA, Concacaf, the UK Prime Minister.
WHAT: Soccer groups criticized Infantino's plan to sell shares of FIFA's tournaments, and demand a full review of his leadership.
WHERE: Statements came from Europe and from North America, Central America, and the Caribbean.
WHY: The plan broke promises of openness, and the groups believe Infantino's leadership no longer puts soccer first.

perspectives.description: Some supporters think Infantino is trying to bring more money into soccer so it can reach more fans and fund new technology and stadiums.
Critics say Infantino is putting profit before the sport, breaking his own promises, and that a full review is the only way to restore trust.
Others are waiting to see if the re-election in March will bring changes, or if Infantino's backers can help him survive the pressure.
